results.result: Eight spontaneous T2DM macaques were identified from 1698 captive rhesus macaques, exhibiting significantly elevated FPG, FPI, and HOMA-IR (p<0.01), indicating insulin resistance, while HbA1c, lipid profiles, and BMI remained comparable to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide consistent physiological characterization of the T2DM macaque model. Statistical significance is reported with appropriate p-values (p<0.01 for metabolic markers, p>0.05 for non-significant parameters), and sample sizes are specified (n=8 per group). The data establish insulin resistance without confounding metabolic syndrome features.

results.result: Gut microbiota composition differed between T2DM and control macaques, with increased Lachnospiraceae (14.48% vs 6.66%) and decreased Lactobacillaceae (20.88% vs 25.95%), and 21 differential microbes identified including elevated Erysipelotrichaceae and Lachnospiraceae members.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C12 demonstrate microbiome alterations using 16S rRNA and metagenomic sequencing with appropriate statistical methods (PCoA, LEfSe). While alpha diversity changes were non-significant (C6), beta diversity and taxonomic composition showed clear differences (C7-C12). Quantitative abundance data and statistical validation support the findings.

results.result: Metagenomic functional analysis identified 74 differential KEGG pathways associated with T2DM and inflammation, and significant upregulation of CAZy enzyme families (CBMs, GTs, CEs, PLs) indicating altered carbohydrate metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 provide functional characterization of microbiome changes. The pathway enrichment analysis (C13-C14) and CAZy enzyme profiling (C15-C16) are appropriate methods with statistical validation shown in Figure 1F-G. The interpretation linking enzyme changes to carbohydrate metabolism is reasonable given the functional roles of these enzyme families.

results.result: Fecal metabolome analysis identified 64 differential metabolites (VIP>1, p<0.05), including significantly decreased anti-inflammatory tryptophan metabolites (muscon, indole-3-acetaldehyde, serotonin) that are AhR ligands, with enrichment in tryptophan metabolism pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C23 describe metabolomic findings with appropriate statistical criteria (OPLS-DA, VIP>1, p<0.05). The identification of AhR ligands (C22) and their anti-inflammatory properties (C20, C23) are supported by citations. However, the functional consequence claim (C23) relies on cited literature rather than direct experimental validation in this study.

results.result: Acylcarnitine metabolites were significantly elevated in T2DM macaques (VIP>1, p<0.1), with l-propionylcarnitine showing the highest increase (FC: 16.19), indicating incomplete LCFA β-oxidation similar to human T2DM.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 establish incomplete fatty acid oxidation through acylcarnitine accumulation. The statistical threshold (p<0.1) is slightly less stringent than other analyses but acceptable for exploratory metabolomics. The interpretation (C27) is supported by mechanistic knowledge (C26) and parallel human findings (C28), though the p-value threshold warrants noting.

results.result: Transcriptome analysis identified 161 DEGs (FDR<0.05) enriched in diabetes-related pathways including insulin resistance, fatty acid metabolism, and inflammation, with specific upregulation of IL6 and IRS1 and downregulation of INSR in the insulin resistance pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 provide transcriptomic characterization with appropriate statistical methods (DESeq2, FDR<0.05) and functional enrichment analysis. The identification of specific pathway components (C34) is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B. Sample size (n=8) and statistical rigor are adequate for RNA-seq analysis.

results.result: WGCNA identified four T2DM-associated gene modules with 546 hub genes (|kME>0.8|), including 102 overlapping DEGs, several of which (IGF2BP2, LEPR, RAP1A, SESTRIN3, ITLN1, ACSM3, HADHB, EFHB) are known T2DM-associated genes in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C42 demonstrate co-expression network analysis with clear methodology (kME threshold) and validation through overlap with DEGs (C40) and literature support for human T2DM associations (C41-C42). The functional annotation of modules (C37-C38) is consistent with the disease phenotype. The analysis appropriately integrates network topology with differential expression.

results.result: Targeted fatty acid analysis detected 34 fatty acids with significantly elevated saturated fatty acids (p<0.05) in T2DM macaques, particularly PA, palmitoleic acid, and oleic acid (p<0.05, VIP>1), with increased plasma PA and decreased fecal PA, consistent with human T2DM.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C49 validate metabolomic findings through targeted analysis with appropriate statistical criteria. The inverse relationship between plasma and fecal PA (C47) suggests enhanced absorption. Parallel findings in human T2DM (C48) and mechanistic literature support (C49) strengthen the interpretation, though sample size appears reduced (n=7-8).

results.result: Inflammatory markers showed significantly elevated IL-1β (p<0.05) but not TNF-α or IL-6 in T2DM macaques, with blood cell analysis revealing increased WBC, neutrophil percentage/number and decreased lymphocyte percentage/number (p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 demonstrate selective inflammatory activation with appropriate statistical validation. The specific elevation of IL-1β (C50, C52) without changes in other cytokines (C51) suggests a particular inflammatory profile. Blood cell count changes (C53) provide additional evidence of inflammation. The selective cytokine response is biologically plausible.

results.result: Correlation analysis revealed significant associations (|r|>0.5, adj p<0.05) between four Lachnospiraceae members (Coprococcus, Lachnospira, Roseburia, Dorea longicatena) and three LCFAs (PA, palmitoleic acid, oleic acid), suggesting Lachnospiraceae participation in LCFA accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 establish microbe-metabolite correlations with appropriate statistical criteria (Spearman correlation, adjusted p-values). However, correlation does not establish causation, and the interpretation of 'participation' (C55) is inferential. The correlation threshold (|r|>0.5) is reasonable but moderate. Additional mechanistic validation would strengthen causal claims.

results.result: FMT from T2DM macaques combined with high PA diet (FTPA) induced prediabetes in mice by day 120 (FPG 6.7 mmol/L), with glucose intolerance, insulin resistance, and elevated body weight, TC, and TG, while FT or PA alone showed only mild effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63 demonstrate causative role of microbiota-PA interaction through controlled FMT experiment. The experimental design with four groups (FTPA, FT, PA, Control) appropriately tests synergistic effects. Statistical significance and diagnostic criteria (FPG ≥6.7 mmol/L for prediabetes) are reported. The requirement for both FMT and PA diet (C63) is critical for establishing mechanism.

results.result: Histopathological examination revealed hepatocyte focal necrosis with inflammatory infiltration and decreased pancreatic islet volume with inflammatory infiltration in FTPA mice, but not in controls or single-treatment groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 provide histological validation of disease phenotype with appropriate tissue examination (H&E staining). The pathological changes are consistent with prediabetes/T2DM and support the metabolic findings. However, quantitative analysis of histological features (islet area, inflammation score) would strengthen the assessment beyond qualitative description.

results.result: PA content was significantly elevated in serum and ileum but decreased in feces of FTPA mice (p<0.05), with upregulated Cd36 expression and reduced IL-17A in ileum (p<0.05), demonstrating that gut microbiota mediated enhanced PA absorption in the ileum.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C75 establish mechanistic pathway for microbiota-mediated PA absorption through compartmental PA measurements and gene/protein expression analysis. The inverse fecal-serum PA relationship (C67-C68) supports enhanced absorption (C69). The Cd36/IL-17A regulatory axis (C70-C72) is supported by citations (C71-C72). The PA-only group control (C73-C74) is critical for establishing microbiota requirement (C75).

results.result: Microbiota analysis of mouse groups showed that FTPA and FT groups shared differential microbes with T2DM macaques (increased R. gnavus, Coprococcus sp.; decreased Christensenellaceae, F16, Treponema sp., F. succinogenes), with Lachnospiraceae abundance increasing over time after FMT, while PA-only group did not replicate these changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 demonstrate successful microbiota transfer and identify specific taxa associated with disease phenotype. The temporal tracking (C80) and cross-species comparison (C82) strengthen causal inference. The PA-only group serving as negative control (C83-C84) is critical for establishing microbiota requirement. Sample size (n=4) is modest but acceptable for microbiome studies.

results.result: The transplanted microbiota from T2DM macaques, particularly increased R. gnavus and Coprococcus sp. and decreased Treponema, F. succinogenes, Christensenellaceae, and F16, promoted PA absorption by regulating IL-17A and Cd36 expression, leading to LCFA accumulation and insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 integrates multiple lines of evidence (microbiome composition, gene expression, metabolite levels, disease phenotype) into a mechanistic model. While the individual components are well-supported, the complete causal chain involves some inferential steps. The model is consistent with all experimental data and provides a testable mechanistic framework.

results.result: Multi-omics analysis of T2DM macaques revealed gut microbiota imbalance (decreased diversity, altered composition), tryptophan metabolism and fatty acid β-oxidation disorders, LCFA accumulation, and inflammation, which were validated through targeted measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91, C121-C122 summarize the multi-omics characterization of T2DM macaques. These summary claims are supported by the detailed findings in earlier claim groups. The integration across omics platforms (16S, metagenome, metabolome, transcriptome) provides comprehensive disease characterization. Validation experiments (C122) confirm key findings.

results.result: Gene expression analysis revealed dysregulation of genes related to lipolysis, fatty acid oxidation, LCFA accumulation, inflammation, and insulin secretion, with downregulated HADHB and ACSM3 causing acylcarnitine and LCFA accumulation and incomplete LCFA oxidation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 integrate transcriptomic and metabolomic data to propose mechanistic pathways. The gene expression changes (HADHB, ACSM3) are consistent with metabolite accumulation (acylcarnitines, LCFAs). However, the causal language ('cause') is inferential rather than experimentally demonstrated through gene manipulation. The model is biologically plausible and consistent with data.

results.result: Decreased Lactobacillus sp. likely caused reduction of AhR ligands (serotonin, indole-3-acetaldehyde), promoting expansion of PA-producing Erysipelotrichaceae and increasing PA levels, with both Erysipelotrichaceae and R. gnavus promoting T2DM through inflammation activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C98 propose a mechanistic pathway linking microbiome changes to PA accumulation and inflammation. While individual components are supported by citations (C95, C97) and correlations, the causal chain is largely inferential (C94, C96 are IMPLICIT claims). The pathway is biologically plausible but lacks direct experimental validation of the proposed sequence. Additional experiments (e.g., Lactobacillus supplementation, Erysipelotrichaceae depletion) would be needed to confirm causality.

results.result: PA accumulation leads to insulin resistance through the PA-mTORC1-Akt pathway, with significantly changed expression of RAP1A, SESTRIN3, and IRS1, and promotes T2DM development by upregulating the NF-κB signaling pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 propose mechanistic pathways for PA-induced insulin resistance. C99 is supported by literature citation, while C100-C101 integrate gene expression data with pathway knowledge. The gene expression changes are documented, but the causal relationships are inferred rather than experimentally validated through pathway manipulation. The model is consistent with established PA signaling mechanisms.

results.result: Gut microbiota mediated PA absorption in the ileum, resulting in serum PA accumulation and T2DM development in mice, with specific microbiota composition (increased R. gnavus, Coprococcus sp.; decreased Treponema, F. succinogenes, Christensenellaceae, F16) involved in the process.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 summarize the causal findings from the FMT experiment. The causative role of microbiota is established through the experimental design requiring both FMT and PA diet. The specific microbiota composition (C105) is identified through comparative analysis across groups. The mechanistic pathway is supported by multiple lines of evidence (PA measurements, gene expression, disease phenotype).

results.result: R. gnavus promotes insulin resistance and inflammation through multiple mechanisms including tryptamine/phenethylamine regulation, mucin degradation, and disruption of intestinal barrier integrity, with decreased IL-17A and increased Cd36 expression indicating microbiota-mediated enhancement of PA absorption.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C114 integrate literature-supported mechanisms (C106-C107, C109, C111-C113) with experimental findings (C110, C114) to explain R. gnavus effects. The mechanistic model linking mucin degradation, barrier disruption, IL-17A reduction, and Cd36 upregulation is biologically coherent. However, direct experimental validation of R. gnavus-specific effects (e.g., through mono-colonization) is not provided.

results.result: Beneficial bacteria (F. succinogenes, Christensenellaceae, F16) that protect mucosal barrier and improve insulin resistance were decreased in T2DM, with collective effects of gut microbes determining PA absorption from ileum to serum and contributing to T2DM development.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 propose protective roles for decreased bacteria based on literature (C115) and integrate findings into a collective microbiome effect model (C116). The decreased abundance of beneficial bacteria is documented, and their protective functions are supported by citations. However, C116 uses cautious language ('might contribute') acknowledging the inferential nature of the collective effect model.

results.result: Spontaneous T2DM macaques provide a valuable model for T2DM pathogenesis investigation, confirming the functional role of gut microbiota and PA in T2DM progression, with specific microbiota composition promoting PA absorption and T2DM development.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 provide concluding statements about model utility and study findings. C117 and C120 are evaluative statements about model suitability supported by the disease characteristics. C118-C119 summarize the causal findings established through the FMT experiments. These conclusions are appropriately supported by the experimental evidence, though C120's claim of 'best' model is subjective.

results.result: Mice transplanted with T2DM macaque fecal microbiota and fed high PA diet developed prediabetes within 120 days.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 summarizes the key experimental outcome demonstrating causative role of microbiota-PA interaction. This is supported by detailed experimental data (C57-C66) showing metabolic, histological, and physiological changes consistent with prediabetes. The 120-day timeframe and experimental design are clearly documented.

results.result: Background literature establishes T2DM as a complex metabolic disease involving gut microbiota, lipid metabolism, and inflammation, with PA being a key LCFA associated with T2DM, but interactions between gut microbiota and LCFA metabolites in T2DM development remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C136 provide literature-based background establishing the scientific context. These claims are supported by appropriate citations and represent established knowledge in the field. C129 and C136 identify knowledge gaps that the study addresses. These background claims appropriately frame the research questions.

results.result: Spontaneous T2DM in macaques is highly similar to human T2DM and represents an optimal animal model, though naturally occurring cases are rare and high-fat diet alone does not reliably induce T2DM, highlighting controversial effects of dietary fat.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C143 establish the rationale for using spontaneous T2DM macaques as a model system. The similarity to human disease (C137, C139) and advantages over other models (C138-C140) are supported by citations. The rarity of spontaneous cases (C141) and failure of dietary induction (C142) are documented in literature, motivating the study's approach. C143 appropriately identifies the need for further investigation.

results.result: Prior studies show insulin-resistant patients exhibit altered fecal metabolites and Lachnospiraceae species overproduce LCFAs during metabolic dysfunction, impairing intestinal integrity, suggesting PA content changes may reflect dynamic equilibrium between host absorption and microbial metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C146 cite recent literature establishing relevant mechanisms, while C147 is an inferential speculation about PA dynamics. The cited studies (C144, C146) provide relevant context for the findings. C147 appropriately uses cautious language ('potentially associated') for the speculative equilibrium model, which is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Eight spontaneous T2DM macaques were identified from 1698 captive rhesus macaques and showed significantly elevated FPG, FPI, and HOMA-IR levels (p<0.01) compared to controls, indicating insulin resistance. However, HbA1c, lipid profiles (TG, TC, HDL, LDL), and BMI did not differ significantly between groups.
results.evaluation: The reviewers describe the work as 'important' and state that 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is convincing.' The comprehensive comparison between T2DM and control macaques is noted as a strength, with no concerns raised about the basic characterization of the T2DM phenotype.

results.result: Gut microbiota analysis revealed that while alpha diversity (Shannon and Simpson indices) decreased in T2DM macaques, this was not statistically significant. However, PCoA showed distinct microbiota composition, with significantly higher abundance of Lachnospiraceae (14.48% vs 6.66%) and lower Lactobacillaceae (20.88% vs 25.95%) in T2DM macaques. Twenty-one differential microbes were identified, including increased Erysipelotrichaceae and five Lachnospiraceae members (R. gnavus, Lachnospira, Coprococcus sp., Dorea longicatena, and Roseburia) in the T2DM group.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'the authors compared comprehensively the gut microbiota...between spontaneous T2DM and the control macaques' as a strength. The editor notes the work 'substantially advances our understanding of the interaction among gut microbiota, lipid metabolism, and the host in type 2 diabetes,' indicating acceptance of the microbiome findings.

results.result: Functional analysis identified 74 differential KEGG pathways between T2DM and control groups, mainly associated with T2DM and inflammation (type II diabetes mellitus, glucagon signaling, starch and sucrose metabolism, lipid metabolism, toll-like receptor signaling). CAZy enzyme families (CBMs, GTs, CEs, PLs) were significantly upregulated in T2DM, indicating changes in carbohydrate metabolism.
results.evaluation: The comprehensive functional analysis is part of the multi-omics approach that reviewers found convincing. The editor's statement that the work 'substantially advances our understanding' and the reviewer's note that 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is convincing' encompasses these functional enrichment findings.

results.result: Metabolomic analysis identified 1564 metabolites in fecal samples, with 64 significantly differential metabolites between groups (VIP >1, p<0.05). Notably, muscon, indole-3-acetaldehyde, and serotonin (anti-inflammatory metabolites and AhR ligands) were significantly lower in T2DM macaques. These differential metabolites were enriched in tryptophan metabolism pathway, and reduced AhR ligands may contribute to inflammation and metabolic syndromes.
results.evaluation: The metabolomic findings are part of the comprehensive multi-omics analysis that reviewers praised. The editor's statement about advancing understanding of 'the interaction among gut microbiota, lipid metabolism, and the host' and the reviewer's comment that evidence is 'convincing' support these metabolite findings.

results.result: Multiple acylcarnitine metabolites were significantly elevated in T2DM macaques (VIP >1, p<0.1), with l-propionylcarnitine showing the highest fold change (FC: 16.19). Acylcarnitines are products of incomplete LCFA β-oxidation that can activate pro-inflammatory pathways and inhibit insulin activity, indicating incomplete LCFA oxidation in T2DM macaques similar to human T2DM.
results.evaluation: These findings are integral to the lipid metabolism dysfunction that reviewers found convincing. The comprehensive metabolomic analysis and its interpretation regarding incomplete fatty acid oxidation are supported by the reviewers' overall positive assessment and the editor's statement about advancing understanding of lipid metabolism in T2DM.

results.result: Transcriptome analysis revealed 161 differentially expressed genes (26 upregulated, 135 downregulated) in T2DM macaques (FDR<0.05), enriched in pathways related to diabetes, fatty acid metabolism, and inflammation. Twenty-six differential pathways were identified by AFC analysis, associated with insulin resistance and inflammation (insulin resistance, PI3K-Akt signaling, bacterial invasion, NOD-like receptor signaling). In the insulin resistance pathway, IL6 and IRS1 were upregulated while INSR was downregulated.
results.evaluation: The transcriptomic analysis is part of the comprehensive multi-omics approach that reviewers found convincing. The identification of gene expression changes related to insulin resistance and inflammation aligns with the reviewers' assessment that the evidence is convincing and the work advances understanding of T2DM pathogenesis.

results.result: WGCNA identified four gene modules related to T2DM: dark green and brown modules (positively correlated) contained genes related to lipolysis and inflammation that were upregulated, while green and darkred modules (negatively correlated) contained genes related to fatty acid metabolism and insulin secretion that were downregulated. Of 546 hub genes identified (|kME>0.8|), 102 were also DEGs, including genes previously associated with human T2DM (IGF2BP2, LEPR, RAP1A, SESTRIN3, ITLN1) and genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation and inflammation (ACSM3, HADHB, EFHB).
results.evaluation: The WGCNA analysis and identification of hub genes strengthen the transcriptomic findings. Reviewers' statement that 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is convincing' and the comprehensive nature of the analysis support these network-based findings linking gene expression to T2DM pathogenesis.

results.result: Targeted fatty acid analysis detected 34 fatty acids in plasma, with saturated fatty acids (SFA) significantly elevated in T2DM (p<0.05) while other types (MUFA, PUFA, N3, N6) showed no significant differences. Specifically, palmitic acid (PA), palmitoleic acid, and oleic acid were significantly higher in T2DM plasma (p<0.05, VIP >1), while PA in stool was decreased. These findings parallel observations in human T2DM.
results.evaluation: The plasma fatty acid findings are explicitly mentioned by reviewers as part of the comprehensive comparison that constitutes a strength of the study. The verification of PA accumulation and its parallel to human T2DM supports the translational relevance that reviewers found convincing.

results.result: PA mediates insulin resistance through three mechanisms: increased diacylglycerol/ceramide synthesis, mitochondrial/ER stress, and pro-inflammatory pathway activation. IL-1β was significantly elevated in T2DM macaques (p<0.05), while TNF-α and IL-6 showed no significant differences. Blood cell analysis revealed increased WBC, neutrophil percentage/number, and decreased lymphocyte percentage/number (p<0.05), indicating inflammation. IL-1β is a key promoter of T2DM systemic and tissue inflammation.
results.evaluation: The inflammatory findings complement the metabolic observations and are part of the comprehensive characterization that reviewers found convincing. The verification of inflammation markers strengthens the mechanistic interpretation linking PA accumulation to T2DM pathogenesis.

results.result: Correlation analysis revealed that four Lachnospiraceae members (Coprococcus, Lachnospira, Roseburia, Dorea longicatena) were significantly associated with PA, palmitoleic acid, and oleic acid (|r|>0.5, adj p<0.05), suggesting Lachnospiraceae participation in LCFA accumulation. Coriobacteriia was also associated with these three LCFAs.
results.evaluation: This correlation analysis linking specific microbes to fatty acid metabolites is central to the study's main finding about microbiota-lipid interactions. The reviewers' statement that the work 'substantially advances our understanding of the interaction among gut microbiota, lipid metabolism, and the host' directly supports these correlation findings.

results.result: In the mouse FMT experiment, FPG levels in FTPA and FT groups increased continuously from day 60, with FTPA reaching 6.7 mmol/L at day 120 (significantly higher than controls), indicating prediabetes development. FTPA mice showed glucose intolerance (OGTT), elevated FPI and ITT indicating insulin resistance, and increased body weight, TC, and TG. FT and PA groups showed weight gain and mild insulin resistance but no significant glucose intolerance or lipid elevation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note that 'verifying the results with macaques in a high-fat diet-fed mice model' is a strength of the study. The successful recapitulation of prediabetes phenotype through FMT validates the causal role of gut microbiota, which reviewers found convincing.

results.result: Histopathological examination revealed hepatocyte focal necrosis with inflammatory cell infiltration commonly in FTPA mice but not frequently in FT and PA groups. FTPA mice showed decreased pancreatic islet volume/area and inflammatory cell infiltration, pathological changes not found in controls.
results.evaluation: The histopathological findings provide tissue-level validation of the metabolic and inflammatory changes. These are part of the comprehensive verification in the mouse model that reviewers identified as a strength, supporting the causal role of microbiota in disease development.

results.result: PA content was significantly higher in serum and ileum but lower in feces of FTPA mice compared to controls (p<0.05), suggesting enhanced ileal PA absorption. Cd36 expression was significantly upregulated in FTPA ileum (p<0.05), while IL-17A (a Cd36 inhibitor) was significantly reduced (p<0.05). The PA-only group showed no significant differences from controls in PA content, Cd36, or IL-17A, indicating that gut microbiota mediated the absorption of excess PA in the ileum.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic finding demonstrating microbiota-mediated PA absorption through IL-17A/Cd36 regulation is central to the study's novel contribution. Reviewers' statement that the work 'substantially advances our understanding' and that evidence is 'convincing' supports this key mechanistic discovery linking microbiota to lipid absorption.

results.result: Microbiota analysis in mice showed lower Shannon and Simpson indices in FTPA, FT, and PA groups versus controls. NMDS indicated distinct composition in FTPA/FT groups, with higher Lachnospiraceae abundance. Three Lachnospiraceae members (R. gnavus/M. gnavus, Coprococcus sp., Clostridium) gradually increased after FMT. FTPA and FT groups shared differential microbes with T2DM macaques (upregulated R. gnavus/M. gnavus and Coprococcus sp.; downregulated Christensenellaceae, F16, Treponema sp., F. succinogenes), while PA group did not share these changes and showed no significant serum PA elevation.
results.evaluation: The successful transfer of specific microbial signatures from T2DM macaques to mice, along with the disease phenotype, validates the causal role of these microbes. Reviewers' positive assessment of the verification in the mouse model and the convincing evidence support these findings demonstrating microbiota transferability and specificity.

results.result: Integration of findings suggests that transplanted microbiota from T2DM macaques, particularly increased R. gnavus/M. gnavus and Coprococcus sp. and decreased Treponema, F. succinogenes, Christensenellaceae, and F16, promoted excess PA absorption by regulating IL-17A and Cd36 expression, leading to LCFA accumulation and insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: This integrative mechanistic conclusion synthesizes the multi-omics and experimental findings. The reviewers' statement that the work 'substantially advances our understanding of the interaction among gut microbiota, lipid metabolism, and the host' and that evidence is 'convincing' directly supports this central mechanistic model.

results.result: Summary of T2DM macaque findings: decreased gut microbiota diversity; upregulated R. gnavus/M. gnavus and Erysipelotrichaceae, downregulated Christensenellaceae; decreased tryptophan and anti-inflammatory metabolites indicating inflammation susceptibility; acylcarnitine accumulation (biomarkers for human T2DM) indicating incomplete LCFA β-oxidation; dysregulated gene expression related to lipolysis, fatty acid oxidation, LCFA accumulation, inflammation, and insulin secretion. Specifically, increased lipolysis and downregulated HADHB and ACSM3 caused acylcarnitine and LCFA accumulation, resulting in incomplete LCFA oxidation.
results.evaluation: These summary findings integrate the multi-omics characterization of T2DM macaques. The reviewers' overall positive assessment, noting that 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is convincing' and the comprehensive nature of the comparison, supports these integrated findings characterizing the T2DM phenotype.

results.result: Mechanistic model proposes that decreased Lactobacillus sp. (an AhR ligand producer) causes reduced AhR ligands (serotonin and indole-3-acetaldehyde), which promotes expansion of PA producer Erysipelotrichaceae, ultimately increasing PA levels. Increased Erysipelotrichaceae and R. gnavus/M. gnavus also promote T2DM development by activating inflammation.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic pathway linking specific microbial changes to metabolite alterations and inflammation is part of the integrative model that reviewers found convincing. The editor's statement about advancing understanding of microbiota-lipid-host interactions supports this mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: PA accumulation leads to insulin resistance by affecting insulin signaling pathway genes. The study demonstrates that significantly changed expression of RAP1A, SESTRIN3, and IRS1 in the PA-mTORC1-Akt pathway causes insulin resistance in T2DM macaques. PA can also promote T2DM development by upregulating the NF-κB signaling pathway.
results.evaluation: These mechanistic findings linking PA to insulin resistance through specific signaling pathways are supported by the transcriptomic data. Reviewers' statement that evidence is 'convincing' and the comprehensive nature of the analysis support these pathway-level interpretations.

results.result: The study determined that gut microbiota mediated excess PA absorption in the ileum, resulting in serum PA accumulation and T2DM development in mice. Specific microbiota composition (increased R. gnavus/M. gnavus and Coprococcus sp.; decreased Treponema, F. succinogenes, Christensenellaceae, F16) was involved in this process. R. gnavus/M. gnavus can promote insulin resistance by regulating tryptamine/phenethylamine content and is a mucin-degrading microbe that increases inflammation.
results.evaluation: This conclusion about microbiota-mediated PA absorption and specific microbial roles is the central finding of the study. Reviewers' statement that the work 'substantially advances our understanding' and that evidence is 'convincing,' along with explicit praise for the verification in the mouse model, strongly supports these conclusions.

results.result: The intestinal mucous layer is an important barrier, and microbiota composition affects its integrity. Increased R. gnavus/M. gnavus suggests higher risk of mucous layer damage. AhR ligand deficiency reduces intestinal mucus production and increases microbial invasion risk, affecting immune cell differentiation and cytokine production. IL-17A regulates fatty acid transporter Cd36, and lipid absorption can be promoted by reducing IL-17A's inhibition of Cd36. Decreased IL-17A and increased Cd36 in prediabetic mice indicated that specific gut microbiota promoted excess PA absorption by disrupting intestinal mucous layer integrity and regulating IL-17A and Cd36 expression.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic model explaining how microbiota affects intestinal barrier function and lipid absorption integrates multiple lines of evidence. The reviewers' positive assessment of the comprehensive analysis and convincing evidence supports this integrative mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: F. succinogenes, Christensenellaceae, and F16 are beneficial bacteria that protect the mucosal barrier and improve insulin resistance. The collective effects of these gut microbes determined excess PA absorption from ileum to serum, which might contribute to T2DM development.
results.evaluation: The identification of protective bacteria and their collective role in PA absorption is part of the comprehensive microbiota characterization. Reviewers' statement that evidence is 'convincing' and the successful demonstration of microbiota effects in the mouse model support these findings about beneficial bacteria.

results.result: The study concludes that spontaneous T2DM macaques (never treated with diabetes drugs) provide a valuable model for understanding T2DM pathogenesis. The study confirms the functional role of gut microbiota and PA in T2DM progression, showing that specific microbiota composition (higher R. gnavus/M. gnavus and Coprococcus sp.; lower Treponema, F. succinogenes, Christensenellaceae, F16) promoted excess PA absorption, which is important for T2DM development. Rhesus macaques may be the best animal model to investigate these relationships given their spontaneous T2DM development.
results.evaluation: These overarching conclusions about the model system and the functional role of microbiota-PA interactions are supported by the comprehensive evidence. The editor's statement that this is 'important work' that 'substantially advances our understanding' and reviewers' note that evidence is 'convincing' support these broad conclusions about the study's contributions.

results.result: Overall study findings: Multi-omics analyses (16S rRNA, metagenome, metabolome, transcriptome) identified gut microbiota imbalance, tryptophan metabolism and fatty acid β-oxidation disorders, LCFA accumulation, and inflammation in T2DM macaques. PA accumulation and inflammation activation were verified. Importantly, mice transplanted with T2DM macaque fecal microbiota and fed high PA diet developed prediabetes within 120 days.
results.evaluation: This summary of the study's main findings integrates the observational and experimental evidence. Reviewers explicitly praised the comprehensive comparison and verification in the mouse model as strengths, and the editor's statement about the work's importance and advancement of understanding supports these integrated findings.

OpenEval provides detailed methodological assessment while peer reviewers emphasize the comprehensive nature and importance of the work.

Full concordance on functional microbiome characterization (C13-C16). Both find the pathway enrichment and CAZy enzyme profiling convincing. OpenEval provides technical validation details while peer reviewers incorporate this into their overall assessment of the multi-omics approach.

Agreement on metabolomic findings (C17-C23). Both evaluations support the identification of metabolite changes and AhR ligands. OpenEval notes reliance on literature for functional consequences (C23), while peer reviewers find the overall metabolomic evidence convincing as part of the comprehensive analysis.

Concordance on incomplete fatty acid oxidation findings (C24-C28). Both evaluations support the acylcarnitine accumulation evidence. OpenEval specifically notes the slightly less stringent p<0.1 threshold, while peer reviewers accept these findings within the broader lipid metabolism dysfunction narrative.

Full agreement on transcriptomic characterization (C29-C34). Both find the RNA-seq analysis with DESeq2 and functional enrichment convincing. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor while peer reviewers incorporate this into their assessment of the comprehensive multi-omics approach.

Complete concordance on co-expression network analysis (C35-C42). Both evaluations support the WGCNA findings and validation through overlap with DEGs and human T2DM associations. OpenEval provides methodological details while peer reviewers find the integrated evidence convincing.

OpenEval notes reduced sample size (n=7-8) and peer reviewers explicitly mention plasma fatty acid findings as part of the comprehensive comparison strength. OpenEval includes C49 while peer review addresses it separately.

OpenEval emphasizes the specific inflammatory profile while peer reviewers incorporate inflammation into the overall disease characterization. OpenEval includes C49 while peer review covers C50-C53.

OpenEval notes that correlation doesn't establish causation and suggests additional validation, while peer reviewers find this central to understanding microbiota-lipid interactions.

OpenEval notes causal relationships are inferred rather than experimentally validated through pathway manipulation, while peer reviewers find the pathway-level interpretations convincing based on transcriptomic data.
